ended: Lost the West Semifinals 2-4 to SA

archetype.name: Early Playoff Exit (second round)
archetype.definition: A solid, honestly earned 49-win team that won a playoff round over a division rival with the better record, then was outclassed by San Antonio and went home a round earlier than the two years before.

report.headline: Same 49 wins, thinner margin, and a second-round wall in San Antonio

recap.finish: 49-33, third in the Northwest; beat DEN 4-2, lost the West Semifinals 2-4 to SA
recap.body:
On paper this was a carbon copy of last year: 49-33 again, a top-ten Net Rtg again, a playoff series won again. Underneath, the edges were softer. Net Rtg slid from 5.1 to 3.3, the site rank from 5th to 8th, and the defense that ranked first two seasons ago and sixth last year settled at eighth, with DRtg climbing from 109 to 111.5 to 113.5. Minnesota was still good, just less the dominant defensive team it had been.

The season had almost no shape, and that was its virtue and its ceiling. After a 2-3 October it won every full month from November through March, reaching 31-19 at the end of January and 46-29 at the end of March, but it never built a run longer than five games and also endured a five-game skid. April was the one soft patch: a 3-4 month allowing 120.57 a game, and a 5-5 close to the schedule. With W vs Pt Diff at exactly 0, the record matched the margin perfectly; 49 wins is what this team was.

The identity was big. The frontcourt graded A and played the bulk of the minutes: Julius Randle led the team in minutes and scored 1,667 points, Rudy Gobert made All-Defensive First Team with a team-best 8.7 Win Shares and a 66.4 TS %, and Naz Reid added 162 threes off the bench. Anthony Edwards was the engine, an All-Star ranked 2nd of 144 on his tab with a 61.7 TS % on a 31.5 USG %, though he played 61 games and his On-Off was flat. The quieter story was Donte DiVincenzo, who played all 82 games and posted the team's best On-Off at 7.6. The wings, by contrast, graded D+, a thin, small-minutes group. The offense shot well (eFG % 6th) but ranked only 12th in rating, with middling turnovers and offensive rebounding eating into the shotmaking, and the defense, for all of Gobert, ranked 20th in DRB % and gave point guards more than almost anyone.

The first round was the best of the year: down 0-1 in Denver against a 54-28 division rival, Minnesota took four of the next five, holding Denver to 96 points twice at home and closing it 110-98 in Game 6. San Antonio was a different problem. A 104-102 steal in Game 1 was followed by a 95-133 rout, and after a Game 4 win evened things at two, the Spurs won the last two by 97-126 and 109-139. Across the playoffs the offense collapsed to an eFG % of 49.5 (13th of 16) with the lowest 3PA Rate of any playoff team, Edwards fell to a 53.3 TS % with a -15.4 On-Off, and Randle managed a 47.9 TS % and a -3.8 BPM. DiVincenzo, listed as out, does not appear in the postseason lines at all.

What survives: a top-rated frontcourt, an All-Star guard and a team whose record was no fluke. What doesn't: a two-year slide in margin and defense, a wing group that graded near the bottom, and a playoff offense that stopped shooting threes and stopped making shots when the opponent got better.

highlights.title: Frontcourt carried the whole build
highlights.body: The A-graded frontcourt was the team: Gobert's 8.7 Win Shares led the roster, Randle logged the most minutes and the second-most points, and Reid supplied spacing off the bench. It held up in the playoffs on the glass, where Minnesota ranked 3rd of 16 in DRB %. Its core pieces played full seasons, so this strength should carry over.

highlights.title: Shotmaking and a top-ten defense
highlights.body: Minnesota's eFG % ranked 6th and its 3P % 6th, while opponents' eFG % ranked 5th lowest, a two-way efficiency profile that kept every full month from November to March above .500. With W vs Pt Diff at 0, the 49 wins were earned by the margin, not close-game luck.

highlights.title: Won a series over Denver
highlights.body: Against a division rival with the better regular-season record, Minnesota dropped Game 1 on the road and then won four of five, holding Denver under 100 twice at home. It was the best basketball of the year and matched the defense-and-size identity.

lowlights.title: Playoff offense dried up
lowlights.body: The postseason eFG % fell to 49.5, 13th of 16, and the 3PA Rate was the lowest of any playoff team, a sharp turn from a regular season built on threes. Edwards' TS % dropped to 53.3 and Randle's to 47.9, and San Antonio won three games by 29 or more points. Without DiVincenzo, who doesn't appear in the playoff lines, the spacing was gone.

lowlights.title: A margin slipping two years running
lowlights.body: Net Rtg has gone from 6.6 to 5.1 to 3.3 over three seasons, and the defense from 1st to 6th to 8th. The record held at 49 wins, but the team underneath it is getting less dominant, and April's 120.57 allowed a game showed how thin the defensive edge had become.

lowlights.title: No wings to speak of
lowlights.body: The wings graded D+, and the whole listed group played a sliver of the minutes the frontcourt did. It also leaked on defense at the point: opponents' point guards scored more against Minnesota than against all but a few teams.

arc.note: After a 2-3 October, Minnesota won every full month through March without ever running away, then faded to 3-4 in April. A first-round win over Denver gave way to a lopsided semifinal against San Antonio.

recap.nextYear: The record is real: W vs Pt Diff of 0 means no close-game luck to give back, so 49 wins is a fair baseline rather than a ceiling. The A-graded frontcourt and Edwards carried it, and DiVincenzo's team-best On-Off suggests his absence mattered as much as anything in May. The work is on the perimeter: a D+ wing group, a defense that gave point guards too much and ranked 20th in DRB %, and a turnover rate that held an elite-shooting offense to 12th in rating. The bigger worry is direction, with Net Rtg and defensive rank sliding for a second straight year, and a playoff offense that stopped taking and making threes against better competition.
